title: Inhalational anthrax: antiphagocytic D-glutamate capsule
vignette: A 34-year-old man comes to the emergency department due to 2 days of fever, malaise, and myalgia. He has also had worsening shortness of breath and cough. The patient works in the mail room at a large company, does not smoke cigarettes, and drinks alcohol occasionally. Chest imaging shows lung infiltrates and prominent widening of the mediastinum. Sputum and blood cultures yield large, gram-positive rods that form colonies resembling a "Medusa head." Which of the following is the most likely bacterial virulence factor contributing to this patient's condition?

clues.note: Mail handling is a classic exposure route for inhaled Bacillus anthracis spores (bioterrorism/contaminated mail) - 'woolsorter's disease' is the occupational analog.
Mediastinal widening (hemorrhagic mediastinitis) with pulmonary symptoms is the hallmark of INHALATIONAL anthrax - spores germinate in mediastinal lymph nodes.

clues.text: large, gram-positive rods that form colonies resembling a "Medusa head."
clues.note: Large boxcar-shaped gram-positive rods forming 'Medusa head' colonies identify Bacillus anthracis, whose key virulence factors are its polypeptide capsule and exotoxin.

whatMatters: Mail-room exposure + fever/cough + WIDENED MEDIASTINUM + large gram-positive rods with 'Medusa head' colonies = inhalational anthrax (Bacillus anthracis). Its distinctive virulence factor is an ANTIPHAGOCYTIC capsule made of D-GLUTAMATE (a poly-D-glutamic acid polypeptide, unlike the polysaccharide capsules of most bacteria). Answer A.
strategy: Identify B. anthracis (Medusa-head colonies, boxcar gram-positive rods, mediastinal widening, spore exposure), then recall its UNIQUE capsule: a poly-D-GLUTAMATE (polypeptide) capsule that is antiphagocytic. Answer A. Reject the polysaccharide capsule (most other encapsulated bacteria), protein A/IgG-binding (S. aureus), polyphosphate granules (Corynebacterium diphtheriae), and flagella (B. anthracis is NONmotile).

eliminations.label: Antiphagocytic polysaccharide capsule - most other encapsulated bugs
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: many bacteria (e.g., Streptococcus pneumoniae) resist phagocytosis via a POLYSACCHARIDE capsule. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: B. anthracis is unusual - its antiphagocytic capsule is a poly-D-GLUTAMATE polypeptide, not polysaccharide. ✅ Correct if: pneumococcus/other polysaccharide-encapsulated organisms.

eliminations.label: IgG-binding outer membrane protein - Staphylococcus aureus (protein A)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: S. aureus protein A binds the Fc portion of IgG, inhibiting opsonization. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: that's a staphylococcal virulence factor, not anthrax's. ✅ Correct if: S. aureus.

eliminations.label: Intracellular polyphosphate granules - Corynebacterium diphtheriae
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: metachromatic (volutin/polyphosphate) granules are seen in C. diphtheriae (Loeffler medium, methylene blue). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: that's a diphtheria feature, not anthrax's virulence factor. ✅ Correct if: Corynebacterium diphtheriae.

eliminations.label: Peritrichous flagella - your pick
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: flagella distributed over the whole cell provide motility (e.g., Proteus). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: Bacillus anthracis is NONMOTILE - it has no peritrichous flagella. The trap is picking a generic virulence-sounding feature. ✅ Correct if: a highly motile organism such as Proteus mirabilis.

reasoning: Mail-room spore exposure + fever/cough + WIDENED MEDIASTINUM = inhalational anthrax
Large gram-positive rods with 'Medusa head' colonies = Bacillus anthracis
B. anthracis's antiphagocytic capsule is uniquely made of poly-D-GLUTAMATE (a polypeptide, not polysaccharide)
mechanism: Bacillus anthracis is a large, nonmotile, spore-forming, gram-positive rod that forms colonies with curled projections ('Medusa head'). Its two principal virulence factors are (1) an antiphagocytic capsule composed of poly-D-glutamic acid (a polypeptide - unusual, since most bacterial capsules are polysaccharide), which blocks phagocytosis, and (2) an exotoxin complex (protective antigen, edema factor, lethal factor). Inhaled spores are carried by alveolar macrophages to mediastinal lymph nodes, where they germinate into vegetative, capsule-producing bacteria; proliferation causes hemorrhagic mediastinitis with the characteristic WIDENED MEDIASTINUM, along with nonspecific flu-like symptoms progressing to shock and death. Exposure classically occurs from contaminated animal products ('woolsorter's disease') or aerosolized spores (bioterrorism, e.g., contaminated mail). The distractors correspond to other organisms: polysaccharide capsule (pneumococcus and others), IgG-binding protein A (Staphylococcus aureus), polyphosphate/metachromatic granules (Corynebacterium diphtheriae), and peritrichous flagella (motile organisms - B. anthracis is nonmotile).
